What does Manton say about how a believer’s experience of God’s grace influences their desire for further communion with Him?

Manton teaches that tasting the Lord’s graciousness creates a yearning for more intimate fellowship. He explains that once a believer has "tasted that the Lord is gracious," this experience "kindles affection, and makes us long for more," leading to a renewed resolution to serve the Lord more faithfully and to walk in holiness. He further notes that "When you find benefit by one duty, it will be an encouragement to come again," indicating that each encounter with divine grace fuels a deeper desire for continued communion.

What does the sermon say about the responsibility of God's people in seeking the salvation of souls and the consequences of failing to do so?

Spurgeon teaches that believers are accountable for earnestly seeking the salvation of souls, warning that neglect brings severe accountability. He states, "if you who are His people are not earnest in seeking the salvation of souls, and they perish, their blood will be required at your hands!" The sermon underscores that while God’s sovereign will ultimately prevails, human earnestness in prayer and evangelism is essential; otherwise, the consequences fall upon the neglectful believers, as illustrated by the example of King Joash deciding whether the Syrians should be beaten three or six times.

What financial advantage does Cotton Mather claim the abolition of Popery would bring to England?

Mather argues that abolishing Popery would be a great economic benefit, noting that “the Abolifhing of Popery in England, is worth at Leaft Eight Millions of Pounds yearly to the Nation.” He presents this as a monetary incentive for embracing the Protestant religion.

According to Gill, how does God's providence relate to natural and necessary actions?

Gill teaches that the providence of God is concerned in all actions, "from the beginning to the end of it," and that He is a "God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed" (1 Sam. 2:3). He explains that every muscular motion—such as birds flying, fish swimming, and humans walking—is continued by God's providence, because all motion ultimately comes from the first Mover, "in whom we live, and move, and have our being" (Acts 17:28). Gill further distinguishes that necessary actions either arise from the necessity of nature or are appointed by God's ordination. This shows that both natural activities and those required by nature are under divine governance.

What covenantal promise does Gill describe regarding believers being adopted as children of God?

Gill teaches that the covenant includes a promise that believers "should be openly adopted, and declared the children of God," meaning that God will treat them as His own offspring, granting them the status of His people, heirs, and portion. This adoption signifies a relational bond whereby God becomes their Father and they become His children, receiving both the discipline of the covenant rod and the inheritance promised to His people.

He includes this detail as part of his brief overview of the appearances made to Abraham and the covenant that followed, emphasizing its role in the doctrine of grace from Abraham to Moses.

According to the 1708 sermon, what are the three distinct ways the Holy Spirit convicts and empowers believers?

The sermon explains that the Holy Spirit convicts and empowers believers in a threefold manner. First, He is described as “the Holy Spirit was to be their Comforter, that they might not be afraid,” providing comfort and courage. Second, He serves as “their Advocate, that they might not be baffled,” defending and guiding them. Third, He operates as a divine power in communication: “When they spoke, there would be a power within them suggesting their words, a power with those words convincing their hearers, and a power in their hearers causing the word spoken to abide in their memories.” In this way the Spirit works within the speaker, persuades the listener, and secures the spoken word in memory.

Why does Manton argue that one must not delay the work of saving one's soul until later in life?

Manton teaches that a person must begin the work of salvation immediately because "death comes by way of surprise; it finds us before we look for it," and postponing it leads to grief when one is too weak to bear it. He warns that waiting until the appointed time "to think of saving our souls" is foolish, likening it to a traveller who sets out at night or the foolish virgins who bought oil too late. The urgency is rooted in the belief that we are sent into the world for not for idle pleasure.

What are the threefold subordination of Christ that Hodge identifies in his commentary on 1 Corinthians 3:23‑63?

Hodge explains that “the Scriptures speak of a threefold subordination of Christ.” He outlines the three aspects as follows: (1) “A subordination as to the mode of subsistence and operation, of the second, to the first person in the Trinity,” which maintains the unity of substance while distinguishing roles; (2) “the voluntary subordination of the Son in his humbling himself to be found in fashion as a man, and becoming obedient unto death,” indicating Christ’s self‑limitation in incarnation; and (3) “the economical or official subjection of the theanthropos,” referring to Christ’s functional role in the redemptive administration.

What does the sermon warn about using encouragements to believe as a 'halfway house' before true faith?

Spurgeon warns that treating encouragements to believe as a provisional resting place is dangerous, stating that "If encouragements to believe are used as a sort of halfway house to rest in before actually believing, they are mischievously used and may ruin our souls!" He illustrates the peril by contrasting this with the example of the afflicted woman who, out of genuine confidence in Christ, pressed directly to the Savior’s garment and was healed. The sermon emphasizes that true faith, not mere encouragement, brings wholeness, and that after such healing a period of fear may follow as a natural response to the joy of salvation.

According to the 1689 Second London Confession, what happened to Christ after his death and before His resurrection?

The 1689 Second London Confession teaches that after Christ’s crucifixion He "remained in the state of the dead, yet saw no corruption" and that "on the third day he arose from the dead with the same body in which he suffered". It further states that He ascended into heaven, now sits at the right hand of the Father, intercedes for believers, and will return to judge men and angels at the end of the world.

What does Spurgeon say about how God protects Christ’s fame against blasphemy and rebellion in Sermon 3436?

Spurgeon teaches that, although Christ is blasphemed by rebels, dishonored by apostates, and grieved by humanity, God will not allow His fame to be tarnished even for a moment. He emphasizes that God has declared, "He has glorified You," and that the Father has exalted the Son with a name above every name that will never be second. Moreover, Spurgeon declares that "God has glorified Him in the entire economy of salvation," ensuring that the crown remains safe upon Christ’s head despite the nations’ rebellion.

How does Manton explain the changing ways in which God is near to His people?

Manton teaches that God’s nearness is not constant in the same manner, but varies according to divine purpose and human experience. He writes that God is “nearer to us sometimes than at others, when we have more evidences of his favour inward or outward,” describing inward evidences as moments when He “quickens, comforts, supports the soul, filleth the heart with joy and peace in believing.” Conversely, he notes that outwardly “sometimes God hideth himself, some times seemeth not to mind the affairs of his people, at other times all the world shall know that they are near and dear to him.” Manton also affirms that while God “is not alike always present with his people, but never withdraweth that influence that is necessary to the being of grace,” He remains ever‑present in a sustaining way. This dynamic picture shows that God’s presence can be felt both in hidden and manifest forms, according to His good pleasure.

According to Spurgeon in Sermon 1064, how is merit treated in the doctrine of salvation?

Spurgeon teaches that merit has no place in the Christian Church and that all salvation is received solely by God’s free favor. He declares that “Merit is an unknown word in the Christian Church--it is banished once and for all” and emphasizes that every blessing comes through grace, not human achievement. Consequently, boasting is excluded because “not of works, lest any man should boast.” In this view the Apostle’s declaration, “By Grace are you saved, through faith, and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God; not of works, lest any man should boast,” underscores that salvation is a gift, not a merit‑based reward.

Why does Calvin describe Abraham as "the father of all them that believe" in his commentary on Galatians and Ephesians?

Calvin teaches that Abraham exemplifies the principle of justification by faith, showing that righteousness comes solely through belief and not works. He points out that Scripture declares "the same are the children of Abraham" and that there is "no variety of roads to righteousness," so Abraham serves as the universal pattern for all believers. Because God justified Abraham on the basis of his faith, Calvin concludes that Abraham is rightly called "the father of all them that believe," (Romans 4:11) and his example establishes the rule for obtaining righteousness for every nation.

What does Perkins’ Golden Chain say are the two parts of the sacramental word, and what roles do they play in a sacrament?

Perkins explains that the sacramentall word consists of two distinct elements: the commandment and the promise. He writes, "The sacramentall word, is the word of institution, the which God after a seuerall manner, hath set downe in each Sacrament." The commandment is the directive by which Christ appoints the administration of the sacrament and the receiving of it, as illustrated in Baptism () and the Lord’s Supper (). The promise, on the other hand, is the assurance that the ordained elements serve as instruments and seals of divine grace, exemplified by the baptismal formula “I baptize thee in the name of the father, of the sonne, and of the holy Ghost.” Thus, the commandment governs the outward act, while the promise secures the inward grace.

What does Edwards say about the reliability of people’s hearts in attaining heaven?

Edwards teaches that many who profess confidence in their own salvation are in fact vulnerable to backsliding and cannot be relied upon to reach heaven, because "the hearts of men are very unsteady; they are not to be trusted." He warns that even those who seem engaged may lose grace when temptations arise, and that without true divine assistance they will be "soon discouraged" and fall into the "fiery billows of God's wrath."

What does the sermon say is necessary to 'lay hold on eternal life' and how is this connected to 'fight the good fight of the faith'?

The sermon teaches that laying hold on eternal life is not a passive or dreamy pursuit; it requires the believer’s utmost energy, personal effort, and the Divine assistance that comes through faith. It stresses that one must "fight the good fight of the faith" by personally possessing the inward life and displaying its power in daily conduct, rather than relying on mere reasoning or scholarly arguments. In other words, the two commands—"fight the good fight of the faith" and "lay hold on eternal life"—are inseparably linked, demanding active, faith‑driven struggle to obtain and live out the divine life.

What does Gurnall say about the insufficiency of moral uprightness that lacks the aim of God's glory?

Gurnall teaches that moral uprightness that is not directed toward the glory of God is merely a partial virtue and therefore falls short of true uprightness. He explains that a person may act faithfully toward an earthly master, yet "God never looked at, or thought of, in all this, and so all worth nothing, because God is left out of the story." The ultimate purpose, he asserts, is to do everything "to the glory of God," quoting 1 Cor. X. 31, "Whatever ye do, do all to the glory of God." Moreover, he cites Eph. vi. 7 that servants must "do their service as to God, not to man;" thus the chief end of any duty is the glorification of God, not merely human approval.

According to Owen, what are the consequences of omitting the first intention of the law and proceeding “per saltum” to the latter?

Owen argues that skipping the first intention of the law and moving “per saltum,” to the latter, turns a law that was “designed for the good of all men” into “the danger of all and ruin of many.” He explains that this practice “takes away all security of their goods and estates” from peaceable subjects, allowing while the owner remains unaware of the cause. Consequently, the legal right to one’s own property is transferred to another, who is then enabled by force to keep it, undermining the principal end of the law to secure each person’s possession of his goods until a lawful conviction.

What metaphors does Swinnock employ to illustrate how ungodly men deceive and prey upon Christians?

Swinnock depicts ungodly men as employing a series of deceptive images: they are; they act "as Butchers, they claw the Ox about the ribs, that they may have the fairer blow at his head"; and he likens them to a pelican that "swalloweth shell‑fish, and warmeth them in her stomach, but it is to make them gape, that she may pick them out of the shels (where they are safe whilst they are shut) and devour them." By using these vivid analogies, Swinnock warns that such men appear sweet or harmless while secretly preparing to trap and devour believers.

What is the first way Spurgeon says people should ‘Come and see’ according to Sermon 633?

Spurgeon teaches that the initial method of ‘Come and see’ is by observation. He urges believers to “give attention to the teaching of the Gospel, to weigh it and prove it.” If the message proves false it must be cast away, but if it is found worthy it should be held fast and never let go.

Edwards argues that the sincerity of God's commands, counsels, and invitations is grounded in what he calls God's perceptive will, not in a deterministic disposing will. Thus, divine commands remain sincere and genuine, despite any underlying necessity.

He warns that allowing every difference or, conversely, forcing all fashionable doctrines on brethren leads to disorder and undermines Christian love. Thus, Manton calls for a balanced forbearance that avoids both extremes.

Which early church fathers does Aa Hodge cite as supporting infant baptism as an apostolic tradition?

In Aa Hodge Outlines Of Theology, Hodge records that several early Christian writers affirm infant baptism as an apostolic tradition. He notes that Justin Martyr (a.d. 138) says, "There were among Christians of his time, many persons of both sexes, some sixty and some seventy years old, who had been made disciples of Christ from their infancy." Irenaeus (born about a.d. 97) declares that "He came to save all by himself; all I say who by him are born again unto God, infants, and little children and youths." Origen (a.d. 185) observes that it was "the usage of the church to baptize infants," and adds that "the church had received the tradition from the apostles." Cyprian (bishop of Carthage, a.d. 248‑258) and his synod mandated infant baptism before the eighth day, and Augustine (a.d. 358) affirms that this "doctrine is held by the whole church, not instituted by councils, but always retained." Thus Hodge presents a continuous patristic witness to infant baptism as apostolic.

What two conditions does Hodge say Roman Catholic theology requires for a sacrament to be efficacious?

Hodge explains that Roman Catholic teaching holds the efficacy of a sacrament on the part of the administrator to two essential conditions. First, the minister must be "canonically authorized"—for the sacraments of orders and confirmation he must be a bishop in communion with the pope, and for the other sacraments he must be a regular popish priest; the personal character of the bishop or priest, even if he be in mortal sin, does not prevent the effect. Second, the minister must exercise the positive intention to do what the church intends, because "To the valid performance of the sacrament is required the intention upon the part of the officiating minister of doing that which the church does."

What warning does Bunyan give about seeking temporal wealth at the expense of one's soul in Life and Death of Mr Badman?

Bunyan warns that the pursuit of temporal gain while sacrificing the soul leads only to loss and damage. What are the two different kinds of lovesickness that Spurgeon describes in his sermon "Heavenly Lovesickness!"?

Spurgeon teaches that heavenly lovesickness appears in two distinct forms. The first kind is the overwhelming delight that floods a believer when he experiences the full enjoyment of Jesus, likened to a bride who is "Stay me with flagons, comfort me with apples: for I am sick of love." In this state the soul is so saturated with divine happiness that the body can barely bear the excess of joy. The second kind is a sorrowful longing, not because the believer has too much of Christ’s love, but because he lacks a conscious awareness of it; the soul is "sick of love" in the sense of yearning for an absent lover. Spurgeon further explains that the first reflects the soul longing for a view of Christ in Grace, while the second reflects the soul that already possesses the view of Divine Grace yet longs for a sight of Christ in Glory.
